docs.title: Welcome to the UPSC PYQ Tracker
docs.text:
An open-source, highly structured repository for UPSC Civil Services Examination (CSE) Mains Previous Year Questions (PYQs).

This platform is designed to move beyond generic answers by providing high-density solution frameworks, examiner-ready data points, and structured value additions mapped directly to the syllabus.

Search & Navigate

Use the Search bar at the top right to instantly find specific topics, thinkers, or keywords (e.g., "Sanskritization", "Balanced Polymorphism", "Self-Help Groups") across all years and papers.

docs.title: 🎯 Anatomy of Our Solution Frameworks
docs.text:
To maximize scoring potential, every PYQ solution here is deconstructed into an analytical, easily replicable format:

  1. Introduction: Precise definitions, origin of concepts (e.g., E.B. Tylor's definitions), or relevant constitutional/historical context.
  2. Body (The Core Demand):
    • Micro-headings directly addressing the question's distinct parts.
    • Value Addition: Explicit integration of data points, specialized italicized terminology, and committee reports (e.g., Xaxa Committee, ARC).
    • Scholar Perspectives: Highlighting key thinkers and ethnographic case studies.
  3. Conclusion: Forward-looking synthesis, contemporary relevance, or multi-disciplinary linkages.

About This Project

This tracker is built on a fast, static engine hosted freely on GitHub Pages. It is designed to be highly readable (try the Dark Mode toggle at the top) and effortless to update.

docs.title: Salient Features of Indian Society, Diversity of India

docs.text:
How do you account for the growing fast food industries given that there are increased health concerns in modern society? Illustrate your answer with the Indian experience. (15 Marks, 250 Words)

View Solution

Introduction

The growth of fast-food industries despite rising health consciousness reflects the paradox of modernity: health awareness is increasing, but convenience-driven consumption is expanding faster. Urbanisation, changing lifestyles, globalisation and aggressive marketing have transformed India's food habits.

Reasons for the Growth of Fast-Food Industries

Mnemonic: FAST FOOD

Factor Explanation with Indian Examples F – Fast-paced lifestyles Dual-income households, longer working hours and time poverty increase demand for ready-to-eat meals. A – Aggressive advertising Celebrity endorsements, influencer marketing and children's food advertising create aspirational consumption. S – Socialisation Fast-food outlets have become youth hangouts and spaces for peer interaction and celebrations. T – Technological change Swiggy, Zomato, UPI and cloud kitchens have made food ordering convenient. F – Foreign cultural influence Globalisation and Westernisation have popularised burgers, pizzas and fried foods. O – Organised retail expansion Malls, food courts, franchises and Tier-2/3 city expansion increase accessibility. O – Offers and affordability Combos, discounts, value meals and low-cost street fast food attract price-sensitive consumers. D – Diversification Indianised menus such as paneer burgers, dosa pizzas and McAloo Tikki adapt global products to local tastes.

docs.title: 2. Why Do Health Concerns Not Reduce Demand?
docs.text:
• Knowledge–behaviour gap: Awareness of obesity and diabetes does not necessarily translate into healthier choices.
  • Instant gratification: Taste, convenience and emotional eating often outweigh long-term health considerations.
  • Health halo effect: Consumers perceive salads, baked products and diet beverages as automatically healthy.
  • Structural constraints: Healthy food may be relatively expensive or less accessible, particularly for working-class urban populations.
  • Normalisation of unhealthy diets: Frequent consumption becomes embedded in family routines and youth culture.

docs.title: 3. Health Implications: The Indian Experience
docs.text:
• Obesity epidemic: NFHS-5 (2019–21) reports 24% of women and 22.9% of men are overweight or obese.
  • Dual burden of malnutrition: Undernutrition and obesity coexist within households.
  • NCD burden: Increased risk of type-2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular diseases and fatty liver.
  • Cultural transition: Traditional diets based on millets, pulses and seasonal foods increasingly compete with energy-dense, nutrient-poor food.
  • Economic consequences: Rising healthcare expenditure and productivity losses.

docs.title: 4. Way Forward: Balancing Industry Growth with Public Health
docs.text:
1. Regulatory intervention: Strengthen FSSAI regulation, nutritional labelling and restrictions on misleading advertisements targeting children.
  2. Behavioural change: Promote dietary literacy through schools, workplaces and public campaigns.
  3. Healthy alternatives: Encourage restaurants to offer affordable, nutritious regional foods.
  4. Industry accountability: Incentivise reduced salt, sugar and saturated fats and healthier product reformulation.
  5. Institutional convergence: Integrate nutrition with preventive healthcare under POSHAN Abhiyaan and Eat Right India.

docs.title: Policy Value Addition
docs.text:
• Eat Right India Movement (2018): FSSAI initiative based on the principles of Eat Safe, Eat Healthy and Eat Sustainable.
  • National Multisectoral Action Plan for Prevention and Control of Common NCDs (2017): Promotes intersectoral action against unhealthy diets.
  • ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines (2024): Emphasise dietary diversity and limiting highly processed foods.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: The objective should not be to eliminate the fast-food industry but to promote responsible food capitalism, where economic growth, consumer choice and public health coexist. India's transition must be from fast food to healthy convenience, without sacrificing its diverse food heritage.

docs.title: High-Value Sociological Thinkers
docs.text:
• George Ritzer – The McDonaldization of Society (1993): Efficiency, calculability, predictability and control increasingly shape consumption patterns.
  • Glocalisation: Global fast-food brands adapt menus to Indian tastes, e.g. McAloo Tikki.
  • Food as an identity marker: Eating out increasingly reflects status, lifestyle and urban aspirations.

docs.title: Answer-Writing Strategy
docs.text:
This is a sociological paradox question. Avoid writing only about the health hazards of junk food.

  • 50%: Explain the industry's growth.
  • 25%: Discuss the health paradox and Indian experience.
  • 25%: Suggest solutions.

Distinctive value addition: Use Ritzer's concept of McDonaldisation to demonstrate sociological understanding.
